newsitem.title: UK: Dollar storms to multi-year high in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar storms to multi-year high in Europe.

text.p: The dollar stormed to its highest level against the mark and Swiss franc in almost three years and its highest level on the yen in four years, spurred by favourable U.S. jobs data and official tolerance of its gains.
The January U.S. employment report proved all things to all markets and U.S. securities in general were immediately in demand after its release.
The dollar benefitted from brisk jobs growth seen in the bigger-than-expected 271,000 rise in non-farm payrolls while a lack of inflationary pressures kept bonds and stocks sweet.
Gains of more than a quarter of a million U.S. jobs in January stands in stark contrast to the 160,000 seasonally-adjusted rise in German jobless during the month.
"The dollar rise is really derived from a bit of everything -- the payrolls data, the bond rally and the G7 meeting," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
"The asset market rally has been a particular driving force today," he said.
U.S. bond and stock markets rose after the jobs data despite the sharp rise in payrolls because earnings data and the unemployment rate showed inflationary pressures remain benign.

"The headline rise in payrolls was sufficiently close to expectations not to disturb existing trends, while the devil was in the detail for bonds, given the softness in earnings and the jobless rate," said Julian Jessop, economist at Nikko Europe.
At 1630 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6722/32 marks, up more than two pfennigs from the close here late Thursday at 1.6512/19 and just off a new 32-month high at 1.6755.
Against the yen, it was at 124.43/48 compared with 123.80/88 late on Thursday and just off a fresh four-year high at 124.72.
The dollar's gains were broad-based. It also set a 33-month high at 1.4460 against the Swiss franc.
Traders were happy to hold dollars going into Saturday's meeting between finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven (G7) most industrialised nations.
Though some concern has recently arisen about G7 objections to the dollar's rise last week, all pre-meeting statements suggest satisfaction with the dollar's rise.
The only word of caution is likely to come in dissuading excess volatiilty, analysts said.
German finance minister Theo Waigel said the dollar's rise "better matches the economic fundamentals. It also strengthens our exports."
Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said the German central bank was also satisfied with the dollar's levels.
"Many U.S. economic data argued in favour of a stronger dollar, and that is what we have now," he told reporters on Friday.

International Monetary Fund head Michel Camdessus told the French daily Le Monde that recent exchange rate shifts make sense and could last. "It is not surprising that the dollar is so robust at a time when the American economy itself is strong," he said.
These comments come against a backdrop of a continued U.S. comittment to its long-standing strong-dollar policy.
Only the Japanese are expected to be a bit cool toward the dollar move but only in relation to the pace and volatility of the unit's rise rather than the direction or level.

"We really don't expect any G7 communiqu as such and while there maybe some accommodation of Japan's wish for more market stability, they won't close the door on dollar gains," said Knuthsen at First Chicago.
Dollar support also came from a conciliatory meeting between German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Italian prime minister Romano Prodi in Bonn, which sharply boosted the lira against the mark.
